pos: n. (Lower Rhine city in the duchy of Cleves; refuge of the Dutch and Walloon exiles, and seat of the convent of 1568)
etymology: German Wesel, from a root meaning a wet meadow or the confluence, the town standing where the Lippe enters the Rhine.
biblical_def: Wesel was a Hanseatic city of the lower Rhine in the duchy of Cleves, and in the middle of the sixteenth century it became the chief landward refuge of the persecuted Reformed of the Netherlands and of the English Marian exiles. Its magistrates let the strangers in, let them worship, and let them organise, and the town earned in the exile literature the name of a hospitable city. From that crowded refugee community came the assembly which matters most. In November 1568, with the Duke of Alva in control of the Netherlands and the Reformed churches there driven underground or abroad, a gathering of ministers and elders at Wesel drew up a body of articles for the ordering of the Dutch Reformed churches—the offices of minister, elder and deacon, the examination and calling of ministers, the keeping of registers, the use of the Heidelberg Catechism and the Belgic Confession, the holding of classes and synods. It was not a lawful synod and it claimed nothing; it was a set of proposals by exiles for a church that did not yet legally exist, and it became the foundation of the church order which the synods of Emden and Dordrecht afterwards completed. The dictionary enters Wesel because a church order was drafted here by men with no buildings, no legal standing and no country, for congregations that were meeting in barns.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a refuge as shelter or protection from danger; hospitable as kind to strangers and guests; and a convent as an assembly of persons devoted to religion.
webster_full: REFUGE, n. [L. refugium.] Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects from danger, distress or calamity.
HOSPITABLE, adj. [L. hospitalis.] Receiving and entertaining strangers with kindness and without reward; kind to strangers and guests.
CONVENT, n. [L. conventus.] An assembly of persons devoted to religion; a body of monks or nuns; the house occupied by such a body.
ORDER, n. Regular disposition; established method; the system by which a church is governed; rule.
STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one unknown; a guest.

Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
corruption_summary: Lower Rhine refuge of the Dutch and English exiles, where the convent of 1568 drafted the church order of a church that did not yet legally exist.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern treatment of church order as a secondary matter, a question of administration to be settled by whatever works. The Wesel articles are the refutation. Men who had lost their houses and their country, who could offer their ministers no salary and their congregations no building, sat down in a refugee town and settled first the offices Christ gave the church, the manner of calling them, and the assemblies by which congregations help one another. They judged that a church without order is not persecuted but dissolved.

The principle to recover is that order is drawn from Scripture rather than from circumstance. “ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee” (Tit 1:5) was obeyed at Wesel in a form that the dictionary, holding congregational government with a plurality of elders, follows in substance though not in every particular. The articles were proposals, acknowledged as such, and were submitted to the churches: a model of how men should legislate for a church they do not own.

pos: n. (Lower Rhine town in the duchy of Cleves; seat of a Reformed university founded under Brandenburg in 1655)
etymology: German Duisburg, from Old High German duis, a marsh or flood-plain, and burg, a fortified place; the town stands where the Ruhr enters the Rhine.
biblical_def: Duisburg was an old imperial town on the lower Rhine which came with the duchy of Cleves to the Reformed Electors of Brandenburg under the Treaty of Xanten in 1614. It had taken the Reformation early and inclined to the Reformed rather than the Lutheran side, and in 1655 the Great Elector gave it the one thing the Reformed churches of the lower Rhine and Westphalia had always lacked: a university of their own. Until then their candidates for the ministry had to travel to Herborn, Heidelberg, Bremen, Franeker or Leiden, which meant that a poor congregation in Cleves or the Mark could not afford to train a minister, and that the men it did send came home with the quarrels of another country. The university of Duisburg served the region for a century and a half, never large and never fashionable, supplying Reformed pastors and schoolmasters to a scattered church in territories where a Catholic or Lutheran prince might hold the next county. The dictionary enters Duisburg for the unglamorous point. The survival of a Reformed church in a divided land depends less on its great men than on whether there is a place within reach where an ordinary pastor's son can be taught Hebrew.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a university as a corporation of persons for instruction in all branches of learning; a candidate as one who seeks an office; and a stipend as a settled pay for services.
webster_full: UNIVERSITY, n. [L. universitas.] An assemblage of colleges established in any place, with professors for instructing students in the sciences and other branches of learning.
CANDIDATE, n. [L. candidatus.] A man who seeks or aspires to an office; one who offers himself or is proposed for preferment.
STIPEND, n. [L. stipendium.] Settled pay or compensation for services, whether daily or monthly wages, or an annual salary.
ELECTOR, n. One who elects or has the right of choice; a prince of the German empire having a voice in the election of the emperor.
DIVIDED, adj. Parted; disunited; distributed; separated into parts.

corruption_summary: Cleves town given a Reformed university by the Great Elector in 1655, so that the lower Rhine could train its own ministers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live temptation is the one Duisburg was founded to answer and which has returned in our own time: a church content to import its ministers from somewhere more impressive. It is cheaper in the short run and ruinous in the long, because men trained in another country's controversies arrive fighting battles their congregations have never heard of, and because a church that does not teach cannot reproduce. The remedy is not a famous faculty; it is a reachable one.

The principle to recover is the apostolic chain of four links: “the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others also. A congregation that cannot name the third and fourth links in its own case has a break in the chain, and a hundred years is long enough for a church to disappear through one.

pos: n. (duchy on the lower Rhine, English Cleves; whose dukes attempted a middle way of reform, and which passed to Brandenburg in 1614)
etymology: German Kleve, from Klippe or kliv, a cliff, the castle rock above the Rhine plain; English Cleves through the French form.
biblical_def: The duchy of Kleve, with Mark, Julich, Berg and Ravensberg, was the greatest of the lower Rhenish principalities, and in the Reformation it attempted something no other state attempted so deliberately: reform without separation. Duke John the Third and his son William issued church ordinances in the 1530s and after which abolished the grosser abuses, provided for preaching and for catechising, regulated the clergy, and refused both the papal and the Lutheran extremes, under the guidance of men formed by Erasmus. For a generation this looked like statesmanship, and historians have called it the Erasmian middle way. It failed. A reform that would not decide the question of authority could not settle any other question, and it left the duchy's churches exposed in both directions: the Reformed congregations grew up outside the ordinance and were persecuted under it, while the Jesuits came in by the court. When the male line failed in 1609 the succession was disputed and the territories were divided by the Treaty of Xanten in 1614, Kleve, Mark and Ravensberg going to the Reformed Electors of Brandenburg and Julich and Berg to the Catholic house of Wittelsbach. The dictionary enters Kleve as the clearest instance of the middle way and of its cost: what began as a refusal to divide ended as a partition settled by armies.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a duchy as the territory of a duke; moderation as the keeping of a due mean between extremes; and an ordinance as a rule established by authority.
webster_full: DUCHY, n. [Fr. duche.] The territory or dominions of a duke; a dukedom, as the duchy of Lancaster.
MODERATION, n. The state of keeping a due mean between extremes; restraint of violent passions; equanimity.
ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; a law or statute.
PARTITION, n. [L. partitio.] The act of dividing; division into shares or parts; separation.
NEUTRAL, adj. [L. neuter.] Not engaged on either side; indifferent; taking no part with either of two contending parties.

corruption_summary: Lower Rhenish duchy whose Erasmian middle way reformed abuses without settling authority, and which was partitioned by the Treaty of Xanten in 1614.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the reform which corrects abuses and leaves the question of authority untouched. The Kleve ordinances abolished real scandals and the dictionary gives them the credit; what they would not do was say whether Scripture or the church's tradition is the judge, and until that is said nothing is settled, because every abuse removed by authority can be restored by the same authority. Erasmus himself is the type of this, and the dictionary names his position as it stands: a lifetime of exposing the follies of the system and a refusal, at the decisive moment, to say which rule governs.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the first question is the standard. “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). A church or a state which postpones that question is not being moderate; it is deferring a decision that its grandchildren will have to take, and they will take it under worse conditions and probably with arms.

pos: n. (Rhine town of the duchy of Cleves, below Wesel; its Latin school a seat of the Brethren of the Common Life)
etymology: German Emmerich, recorded as Embrica, probably from a personal name with the Germanic -ik; the town stands on the right bank of the Rhine near the Dutch border.
biblical_def: Emmerich is a Rhine town of the old duchy of Cleves, with a collegiate church of St Martin and, from the fifteenth century, a Latin school which was one of the northern schools shaped by the Brethren of the Common Life. That movement—the Devotio Moderna of Groote and Thomas a Kempis—ran a chain of such schools down the Yssel and the lower Rhine, at Deventer, Zwolle, Emmerich and elsewhere, and in them the sons of ordinary burghers learned good Latin, read the Scriptures and the fathers rather than the schoolmen, and were taught a plain, inward, unceremonious piety. Almost every figure of the northern Renaissance and a great many of the first Reformation generation passed through one of these houses. Emmerich's school was still drawing scholars in the sixteenth century, and the town afterwards held Reformed and Roman congregations side by side under Brandenburg rule. The dictionary enters Emmerich to make a point about the Devotio Moderna which is often missed. The Brethren were not Protestants and would have been shocked to be called so; they did not touch the doctrine of justification. What they did was teach two generations of boys to read the Bible in a good text and to distrust religious machinery, which turned out to be enough to make the Reformation possible.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines devotion as the state of being dedicated to God, religious worship; a brotherhood as an association of men for a common purpose; and to educate as to bring up and instruct.
webster_full: DEVOTION, n. [L. devotio.] The state of being dedicated or consecrated; piety; religious worship or exercises; ardent love or affection.
BROTHERHOOD, n. An association of men for any purpose; a fraternity; the state of being a brother.
EDUCATE, v.t. [L. educo.] To bring up, as a child; to instruct; to inform and enlighten the understanding; to cultivate and train.
LATIN, adj. Pertaining to the Latins, a people of Latium in Italy; the language of the ancient Romans.
PREPARATION, n. The act of preparing or fitting for a particular purpose; that which is prepared.

corruption_summary: Cleves Rhine town whose Latin school under the Brethren of the Common Life taught boys to read the Scriptures and distrust religious machinery.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The honest difficulty is the Devotio Moderna's own doctrine. Its piety was inward and its ethics were high, and it left the medieval scheme of merit substantially untouched; the Imitation of Christ, its most famous book, can be read through without learning that a sinner is justified by faith alone in the imputed righteousness of Christ. The dictionary therefore refuses both the Roman claim that the Brethren show the old church reforming itself without need of a Reformation, and the Protestant claim that they were Protestants before the name.

The principle to recover is the preparatory value of plain learning. “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) was the habit these schools formed in boys who did not yet know what they would find; and when the doctrine came, in the 1520s, it came to men who had been taught to check it against a text. A church that forms that habit in its children has done something whose value it will not see for twenty years.

pos: n. (small county on the left bank of the lower Rhine, which came to the house of Orange-Nassau and held the Reformed religion)
etymology: German Moers, earlier Murse, from a root for a marsh or moor, the county lying in the wet ground west of the Rhine.
biblical_def: Moers was one of the small imperial counties of the lower Rhine, a town and a few villages on the left bank opposite Duisburg, and its church history is the history of what a very small territory can do when its lord is of the religion. The county passed by inheritance into the orbit of the house of Orange-Nassau, which took possession at the turn of the seventeenth century, and under that protection the Reformed religion was established, a Reformed church order on the Dutch model was set up, and the town became a place where Reformed worship was legally safe within a day's walk of territories where it was not. In the long contest on the lower Rhine between Spain, Brandenburg, the Dutch Republic and the Catholic princes, such small protected enclaves did work out of all proportion to their size: they kept the classes meeting, held the registers, trained and sheltered ministers for places where ministers could not live, and gave a congregation somewhere to carry its children for baptism. Moers afterwards passed to Prussia. The dictionary enters it for that function, which has no glamour and no great names. A church that survives a long persecution usually turns out to have had a small safe place nearby, and somebody's inheritance was the reason.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a county as a circuit or district under a count; an enclave as a territory surrounded by another; and protection as defense, shelter from evil.
webster_full: COUNTY, n. [Fr. comte.] Originally, an earldom; a circuit or portion of a kingdom, into which the whole is divided for the purposes of government.
ENCLAVE, n. A place or country entirely surrounded by the territory of another; an isolated possession.
PROTECTION, n. [L. protectio.] Defense; shelter from evil; preservation from loss, injury or annoyance; that which protects.
INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; that which is inherited; a possession.
REGISTER, n. A written account of acts, judgments or proceedings, preserved as authentic evidence; a book of record.

corruption_summary: Small lower Rhenish county under Orange-Nassau protection, whose legally safe Reformed worship served a church persecuted all around it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live difficulty is a real one and the dictionary states it. A church protected by a prince is a church whose legal existence depends on a marriage settlement and a succession, and when the inheritance changes the protection ends; the lower Rhine is full of territories which changed religion twice in a century because a count died childless. The arrangement is therefore a mercy and not a foundation, and a congregation which forgets the difference will be destroyed by the next will that is read.

The principle to recover is the doctrine of the remnant and of the prepared place. “And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she hath a place prepared of God” (Rev 12:6) is the church's normal condition in a hostile age, and the place is usually unimpressive. The dictionary holds that God preserves his church ordinarily by such means—a small county, a tolerant magistrate, a border a day's walk away—and that these are providences and ought to be named as such rather than credited to the family that happened to own them.

pos: n. (Westphalian town, Burgsteinfurt, seat of the Reformed high school founded by the counts of Bentheim in 1588)
etymology: German Steinfurt, the stone ford, from Stein, a stone, and Furt, a ford; Burg for the moated castle of the counts.
biblical_def: Burgsteinfurt was the residence of the counts of Bentheim-Steinfurt in the far west of Westphalia, and in 1588 Count Arnold the Fourth founded there a high school—a gymnasium illustre, a college between a Latin school and a university, which could teach philosophy and theology and prepare men for the ministry though it could not grant the doctorate. It was deliberately Reformed, it drew teachers and students from the Netherlands and the Rhineland, and for a century it was one of the handful of places where a Reformed minister could be trained between the Yssel and the Weser. Such schools are a particular feature of the Reformed territories of north-west Germany, where no prince was rich enough for a university and every county needed ministers: Herborn in Nassau, Burgsteinfurt in Bentheim, the Bremen gymnasium, the Hanau and Zerbst schools. Steinfurt's later history followed its county's: when the house turned Catholic in the second half of the seventeenth century the school suffered, and it never recovered its first standing. The dictionary enters it for the type. A small Reformed state's most durable act was almost always to found a school, and the school usually outlasted both the dynasty and the policy that made it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a gymnasium as a place of exercise or instruction; a count as a nobleman equal in rank to an earl; and endowment as the bestowing of a permanent fund.
webster_full: GYMNASIUM, n. [Gr. to exercise.] A place where athletic exercises are performed; in Germany, a high school or seminary of learning preparatory to the university.
COUNT, n. [L. comes.] A title of foreign nobility, equivalent to the English earl; the governor of a county.
ENDOWMENT, n. The act of settling a fund or permanent provision for the support of a school, church or charitable institution.
SEMINARY, n. [L. seminarium, a seed-plot.] A place of education; a school, academy or college for the instruction of youth.
FOUND, v.t. [L. fundo.] To set, to establish; to lay the basis of; to begin and build, as an institution.

corruption_summary: Westphalian town whose Reformed high school of 1588 trained ministers for a region with no university, and declined when its county turned Catholic.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the habit of judging a church's theological education by the prestige of its institutions. On that measure Burgsteinfurt was nothing: a count's school in a small Westphalian town, with no doctorate to confer and a few score students. By the measure that matters—whether the congregations within reach had taught ministers—it did the work of a university for a century, which is more than can be said for some universities.

The principle to recover is the duty of provision. “as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies” (Ecc 12:11) describes a settled teaching ministry, and such a ministry has to be paid for and prepared somewhere. The dictionary holds that endowing a school is among the most useful things wealth can do for a church, and notes the warning in Steinfurt's decline: an institution dependent on one family's confession is at the mercy of one family's conversion.

pos: n. (Westphalian county on the Dutch border, made Reformed by Count Arnold the Fourth and turned Catholic by his descendant in 1668)
etymology: German Bentheim, from Benta, a stream-name, and heim, a home or settlement; the county lies about the sandstone ridge west of the Ems.
biblical_def: The county of Bentheim lay on the Dutch border between the bishopric of Munster and the province of Overyssel, and it is the clearest small example in Germany of the principle that whoever rules determines the religion, applied twice in a hundred years in opposite directions. Count Arnold the Fourth, who ruled from 1562 and whose lands included Steinfurt and Tecklenburg, brought his territories from the Lutheran to the Reformed confession in the 1580s, introduced a Reformed church order, catechism and discipline, and founded the high school at Burgsteinfurt in 1588 to supply it with ministers. For two generations Bentheim was a Reformed county with close ties to the Dutch churches across the border. Then in 1668 Count Ernst Wilhelm, having turned Roman Catholic, set about restoring the old religion in his lands: churches were taken, Reformed ministers removed, and the subjects pressed. The attempt did not wholly succeed, because the people had been catechised for eighty years and because the Dutch Republic next door made its displeasure felt, but the county was left permanently mixed. The dictionary enters Bentheim as a standing argument against the whole system by which a prince's conscience settles his subjects' worship.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conscience as the faculty by which we judge of the rightness of our own actions; conformity as compliance with an established form; and compel as to drive or urge irresistibly.
webster_full: CONSCIENCE, n. [L. conscientia.] Internal or self-knowledge; the faculty, power or principle which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our own actions.
CONFORMITY, n. Correspondence with a model or pattern; compliance with an established form, rule or practice, as in religion.
COMPEL, v.t. [L. compello.] To drive or urge with force, or irresistibly; to constrain; to oblige; to necessitate.
SUBJECT, n. One that owes allegiance to a sovereign and is governed by his laws; one under the dominion of another.
CATECHISE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions and receiving answers, particularly in the principles of the Christian religion.

Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
Mat 5:10

corruption_summary: Westphalian border county made Reformed in the 1580s and pressed back toward Rome by its count in 1668, leaving it permanently mixed.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the territorial principle itself—the rule, written into the imperial settlements, that the religion of a land follows the religion of its prince. It was adopted as a peace formula and it worked as a peace formula; what it does to the subject is to make his worship a function of a dynasty's private convictions. Bentheim shows both halves. Arnold the Fourth used the principle for the truth and the dictionary is glad of the result; Ernst Wilhelm used the same principle for error, and the second use is the refutation of the first.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the limit of the magistrate and the freedom of conscience in the worship of God. Scripture requires subjection to the higher powers and nowhere gives them the keys. The dictionary also records what actually blunted the counter-reformation here: “Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6) had been obeyed for eighty years, and a catechised people is harder to turn than a conforming one.

pos: n. (Westphalian county between the Weser and the Teutoburg forest, brought to the Reformed confession by Count Simon the Sixth)
etymology: German Lippe, from the river Lippe, a name of Celtic or early Germanic origin; the county took its name from the lords of Lippe.
biblical_def: The county of Lippe lay between the Weser and the Teutoburg forest, and it took the Reformation in the Lutheran form in the middle of the sixteenth century. Count Simon the Sixth, who ruled from 1563, was a learned prince in correspondence with the Reformed theologians of the Rhine, and about the turn of the seventeenth century he carried his county over from the Lutheran to the Reformed confession—the step German historians call a second reformation, by which several princes of the Empire moved their lands from Wittenberg to Heidelberg. In Lippe, as elsewhere, it was easier to decree than to accomplish. The town of Lemgo, the largest in the county, refused: it held to the Augsburg Confession and to its Lutheran ministers, resisted the count's church ordinance, and after a long dispute the two sides came to a written settlement by which Lemgo kept its Lutheran religion inside a Reformed county. Thereafter Lippe was Reformed and Lemgo was not, and both remained so for three hundred years. The dictionary enters Lippe for that outcome, which is more instructive than a clean victory. A prince carried his territory and a single stubborn town would not be carried, and the settlement which admitted the fact was wiser than the decree which had denied it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confession as a formulary of the articles of faith; conformity as compliance with an established form; and a settlement as an adjustment of differences.
webster_full: CONFESSION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a public avowal of belief.
CONFORMITY, n. Compliance with an established form, rule, practice or custom, particularly in religion.
SETTLEMENT, n. The act of settling; adjustment of differences; a final agreement between parties in dispute.
STUBBORN, adj. Unreasonably obstinate; inflexible; not to be moved or persuaded by reasons; hence, persevering.
DECREE, n. [L. decretum.] Judicial decision; an order, edict or law made by a superior as a rule to govern inferiors.

Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: Westphalian county carried from the Lutheran to the Reformed confession about 1600, except for the town of Lemgo, which refused and kept its own.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The genuine question is whether the second reformations were a reform or an imposition, and the dictionary answers it in two parts. The doctrine the Reformed princes adopted was the truer doctrine, and the dictionary holds it—on the Supper, on the second commandment and images, on election. The means were wrong: a confession is a thing a church receives and subscribes, not a thing a prince decrees for his subjects, and where the two are confused the resulting conformity is worth very little.

The principle to recover is in the apostle's word to a congregation rather than to a court: “Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught” (2Th 2:15). Lemgo did exactly that. The dictionary does not agree with what Lemgo was holding, and notes that it held it in the right way—by the town's own conviction, against its prince, at cost—while the rest of the county received the better doctrine in the worse manner.

“Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1) — and a confession is not among the things a prince may decree.
“Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9) — a Reformed county with a Lutheran town in it for three hundred years.

pos: n. (residence of the counts of Lippe in the Teutoburg forest; seat of the Reformed consistory of the county)
etymology: German Detmold, recorded as Theotmalli, from Old Saxon thiod, a people, and mahal, an assembly place—the people's meeting-place.
biblical_def: Detmold is the old residence town of the counts of Lippe, at the foot of the Teutoburg forest, and its name means the place where the people assembled. It became the administrative centre of the county's Reformed church after Simon the Sixth brought Lippe over to that confession about the turn of the seventeenth century: the consistory sat here, the ministers were examined and ordained here, the visitations of the country parishes were ordered from here, and the county's registers and church records were kept here. That is the whole of its church history and it is worth an entry, because the apparatus of a small established church is the part no one writes about and the part that does the work. A consistory which meets, examines candidates, hears complaints against ministers, keeps the marriage and baptismal registers, and sends men out to look at the country parishes once in three years is the difference between a confession written in a book and a confession actually taught in two hundred villages. The dictionary enters Detmold for the drudgery. The records of such a body are dull reading and they are the most honest evidence that exists about whether a church was doing anything.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a consistory as an ecclesiastical court or assembly; visitation as the act of a superior who inspects churches; and a register as a book of record.
webster_full: CONSISTORY, n. [L. consistorium.] A place of justice in the spiritual court; an assembly of ecclesiastical persons for the regulation of church affairs.
VISITATION, n. The act of a superior or superintendent who visits churches or schools to inspect their state and proceedings.
REGISTER, n. A written account or entry of acts, judgments or proceedings, preserved as authentic evidence of facts.
EXAMINE, v.t. [L. examino.] To inspect carefully; to interrogate, as a witness or a candidate; to try by a rule or law.
DRUDGERY, n. Hard labor; ignoble toil; work that is mean and laborious.

Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Neh 4:6
So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work.
corruption_summary: Lippe residence town where the Reformed consistory sat, examined ministers, kept the registers and ordered the visitation of two hundred villages.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the romantic account of church life in which everything is revival, preaching and conflict, and nothing is administration. It produces congregations which cannot find their own minutes, do not examine the men they call, and discover a scandal five years after everyone concerned has left. The records of a consistory are the church's memory, and a church without a memory repeats every error it has ever made.

The principle to recover is that oversight is a real duty with real paperwork. “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28) is addressed to elders and includes the unglamorous half: knowing who is in the flock, who has been admitted, who has been disciplined, and who is preaching in the next village. “So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof” (Neh 4:6) is the picture—a joined wall, built by people who kept account of what had been built.

“So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof” (Neh 4:6) — registers, minutes and the church's memory.

pos: n. (residence of the counts of Schaumburg in Lower Saxony; its town church of 1615 built as an example of religion and not of architecture)
etymology: German Bückeburg, from Bücke, a local water-name, and Burg, a fortified seat; the town grew about the moated castle in the marsh.
biblical_def: Buckeburg was the residence of the counts of Schaumburg, a small Lower Saxon house whose territory lay west of Hanover, and under Count Ernst, who ruled from 1601, it was rebuilt as a princely town. The count was a Lutheran of the sort the age produced in the small states: a builder, a founder of schools, and a man who meant his buildings to argue. The town church, raised between 1611 and 1615, is one of the earliest Protestant churches in Germany built new for Protestant worship rather than inherited and adapted, and across its front the count set an inscription declaring the work an example of religion and not of architecture. The claim is worth examining rather than admiring, because the facade is in fact an elaborate piece of architecture and the sentence was carved in stone at considerable expense. The dictionary enters Buckeburg for that tension, which is instructive and not merely amusing. Protestant church building has always had to answer the question the inscription raises: a congregation must meet somewhere, the building will say something whether or not it is meant to, and the honest course is to decide what it should say rather than to pretend it says nothing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines architecture as the art of building according to rules; an inscription as something written or engraved on a solid substance; and ornament as that which embellishes.
webster_full: ARCHITECTURE, n. [L. architectura.] The art of building; particularly, the art of constructing houses, churches and other buildings for the purposes of civil life, according to rule.
INSCRIPTION, n. [L. inscriptio.] Something written or engraved; a title; a word or words written or engraved on a solid substance for perpetuity.
ORNAMENT, n. [L. ornamentum.] That which embellishes; any thing which adds to beauty or elegance; decoration.
EDIFY, v.t. [L. aedifico.] To instruct and improve the mind in knowledge generally, and particularly in moral and religious knowledge.
PLAINNESS, n. The state of being plain or level; want of ornament; openness; sincerity; simplicity of style.

Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.
corruption_summary: Schaumburg residence whose new Protestant town church of 1615 carried an inscription declaring it an example of religion and not of architecture.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live corruption is in both ditches. On one side, the building made an argument for the prince who paid for it, so that the congregation worships inside a monument to a family; on the other, the affectation of plainness, in which great care and money are spent to achieve an appearance of carelessness, and the people are invited to admire the humility of the room. Buckeburg's inscription is a fair specimen of the second while the facade is a specimen of the first.

The principle to recover is that the church is people and not masonry. “the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15) names a congregation, not a building, and “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14) settles the question of permanence. The dictionary holds that a meeting-house should be sound, decent, audible and cheap, that the money saved belongs to the poor and to the ministry, and that no inscription makes a building modest.
